topic: The Bloop: The Ocean Sound Nobody Could Explain
method: Web search and page reads of NOAA primary pages, peer-reviewed papers (abstracts and open PDFs), and news coverage. Every factual statement below cites claim IDs in claim_ledger.json, which cite sources.json. Distances were computed by us (great-circle, haversine, mean Earth radius 6,371 km) from the published coordinates.
one_paragraph_summary: In the northern summer of 1997, a civilian NOAA hydrophone array in the eastern equatorial Pacific, built to listen for seafloor earthquakes and volcanoes, repeatedly recorded a loud, low sound whose pitch rose over about a minute. Sped up 16 times so people could hear it, it became the 'Bloop'. NOAA first placed it roughly at 50°S 100°W and listed its origin as unknown; its scientists suspected Antarctic ice as early as 2001, yet also said its shape resembled an animal call. Media and the internet turned it into a sea-monster story, later tied to Lovecraft's Cthulhu and a 2012 fake mermaid documentary. After NOAA deployed hydrophones off the Antarctic Peninsula (2005-2009) and recorded thousands of icequakes, PMEL concluded the 1997 sounds are consistent with icequakes from large icebergs cracking and fracturing, with an arrival direction pointing to the Antarctic margin. The icequake explanation is strongly supported but rests on comparison and direction; no one saw the event and the exact iceberg is unknown.

timeline.event: Lovecraft's 'The Call of Cthulhu' (Weird Tales) places the sunken city R'lyeh at 47°9'S 126°43'W.
Ewing and Worzel demonstrate long-range sound in the deep sound (SOFAR) channel.
NOAA PMEL begins continuous autonomous hydrophone monitoring in the eastern equatorial Pacific.
'Slow Down' recorded (later attributed to an iceberg running aground off the Antarctic Peninsula).
The 'Bloop' is recorded repeatedly; pitch rises over ~1 minute; heard on multiple sensors >5,000 km away; general location ~50°S 100°W; origin unknown.
'Julia' recorded (later attributed to a grounded iceberg off Antarctica).
Christopher Fox tells CNN the team suspects ice off Antarctica; in an August 2001 NOAA release he still lists the Bloop's origin as undetermined.
New Scientist reports Fox's 'hunch' that the Bloop is the most animal-like of the unidentified sounds; giant-squid / sea-monster coverage follows.
Cryptozoologist Loren Coleman says it most likely comes from a marine beast.
NOAA National Ocean Service says the source was found in Antarctica in 2005.
Dziak's team deploys autonomous hydrophones in the Bransfield Strait (arrays run to 2009 with Scotia Sea).
Icequakes very similar to the Bloop used to track iceberg A53a breaking up near South Georgia.
NASA APOD says no further Bloops have been heard since 1997.
Animal Planet airs the fictional 'Mermaids: The Body Found', which uses the Bloop as a springboard.
NOAA states no evidence of aquatic humanoids has ever been found.
WIRED UK: Dziak confirms the Bloop matches Antarctic icequakes; tens of thousands occur yearly.
Dziak et al., 'Life and Death Sounds of Iceberg A53a' (Oceanography).
Dziak et al. (PLoS ONE): icequakes are a prominent feature of the Antarctic Peninsula soundscape.

the_original_evidence.instrument: NOAA PMEL Equatorial Pacific autonomous hydrophone array: moored hydrophones recording low-frequency sound in the SOFAR channel (not the Navy SOSUS network itself).
the_original_evidence.what_was_recorded: A broad-spectrum, low-frequency signal rising rapidly in pitch over about one minute; recorded repeatedly in summer 1997; heard on multiple sensors at ranges over 5,000 km.
the_original_evidence.what_the_public_hears: A 16x sped-up clip (NOAA PMEL WAV/MP3). The speed-up compresses a minute into a few seconds and raises the pitch, which makes it sound like a creature's 'bloop'.

location.later_assessment: Arrival azimuth points to the Antarctic margin: between Bransfield Strait and the Ross Sea, possibly Cape Adare (NOAA PMEL).
location.uncertainty: A bearing defines a line, not a point; the candidate coastline spans thousands of kilometres. The precise source and iceberg were never identified.

not_in_the_record: A measured source level (dB) for the Bloop
A peer-reviewed paper analysing the 1997 signal itself
Any visual observation of the event

the_investigation.summary: NOAA's scientists suspected ice early but could not confirm it. They later recorded the Antarctic soundscape directly (Bransfield Strait and Scotia Sea, 2005-2009), found that icequakes are common and loud, tracked iceberg A53a by its sound in 2008, and found icequake spectrograms very similar to the Bloop. Combined with the arrival direction, this led PMEL to describe the Bloop as consistent with icequakes from large icebergs.
the_investigation.independent_support: Other teams detected Antarctic iceberg sounds at great ranges: Ross Sea icebergs heard in French Polynesia (Talandier et al. 2002); B15a and C19a heard ~10,000 km away (Matsumoto et al.).
the_investigation.sister_signals: 'Slow Down' (1997) and 'Julia' (1999) were also attributed to grounded icebergs off Antarctica.

discrepancies_found: Location: 50°S 100°W (early NOAA page) vs. a bearing toward Bransfield Strait–Ross Sea–Cape Adare (later NOAA page).
Distance figures: sensors >3,219 km apart (NOS), up to 4,800 km apart (New Scientist), heard at >5,000 km (PMEL) — different measures.
Solved date: 2005 (NOS) vs. 2008 data (PMEL) vs. 2012 public confirmation (WIRED UK).
Mechanism wording: 'breaking away from an Antarctic glacier' (NOS) vs. 'icebergs as they crack and fracture' (PMEL).
'Slow Down' location: 15°S 115°W (early page) vs. 62°S 60°W (PMEL data page).
A 2001 NOAA release quotes Fox saying the Bloop had been reported 'for decades by Navy sonar men' — unsupported elsewhere; not used.
Fox in 2001 (suspects ice) vs. 2002 (most animal-like of the unknown sounds) — both reported; the script should show this honest uncertainty.
open_questions: Which iceberg, and exactly where? Unknown; likely unknowable from the 1997 data alone.
Was there ever a formal NOAA analysis of the 1997 Bloop? We found none; the conclusion is published only on NOAA web pages and in interviews.
Original (non-sped-up) Bloop audio: is a real-time file available from NOAA? Only the 16x versions were found.

authentic_material_available: NOAA PMEL 16x Bloop audio (WAV 162k; Ocean Explorer MP3 452k) — U.S. federal work, generally public domain; verify credit lines
NASA Landsat Antarctica mosaic (used by NOS) — NASA, generally public domain

story_angles: Hook: the clip everyone knows is a lie of speed — a one-minute groan squeezed into a 'bloop'.
Twist structure: the scientists suspected ice almost from the start; the mystery was bigger in public than in the lab.
Human detail: twice NOAA went listening for volcanoes and heard ice instead (1997 Pacific; 2005 Antarctica).
Myth anatomy: how 'unknown' became 'monster' (2002 headlines → Cthulhu coordinates → 2012 fake mermaid documentary).
Honest verdict: strongly supported icequake, not a witnessed event; the deeper story is how loud a warming polar ocean is.
visual_implications_for_storyboard: Real: NOAA audio, our spectrogram/waveform built from it, maps from public data (coordinates, bearings, distances computed here).

Reconstruction (labelled): moored hydrophone in the SOFAR channel, sound propagation across the Pacific, Antarctic iceberg cracking underwater, iceberg A53a drifting near South Georgia, deep empty ocean at 50°S 100°W.

Myth segment: no creature reconstructions that could be taken as real. Use stylised archival-type headlines recreated as clearly labelled graphics with no fake mastheads, a book/page treatment for Lovecraft's 1928 text, and abstract silhouettes that dissolve into ice.
